official_requirement: Show understanding of binary magnitudes and the difference between binary prefixes and decimal prefixes.
official_notes: Use and distinguish kibi/kilo, mebi/mega, gibi/giga and tebi/tera; binary prefixes use powers of 1024 and decimal prefixes use powers of 1000.

official_requirement: Show understanding of binary, denary and hexadecimal number systems, BCD, and one's- and two's-complement representations.
official_notes: The Version 2 row requires binary, denary, hexadecimal, Binary Coded Decimal (BCD), one's complement and two's complement; BCD and complements are representations rather than additional number bases.

official_requirement: Convert an integer value from one required number base or representation to another.
official_notes: Conversions apply to integer values and the binary, denary, hexadecimal, BCD, one's-complement and two's-complement representations named in the preceding Version 2 row.

official_requirement: Perform binary addition and subtraction using positive and negative binary integers.
official_notes: Version 2 explicitly requires both addition and subtraction using positive and negative binary integers; fixed-width representation must be retained throughout a calculation.

official_requirement: Show understanding of how overflow can occur in fixed-width binary arithmetic.
official_notes: Overflow occurs when the mathematical result is outside the range representable by the stated bit width and representation; it is not inferred from every internal carry or from a leading 1 alone.

official_requirement: Describe practical applications where BCD and hexadecimal are used.
official_notes: Candidates must connect each representation to a practical use and explain why it suits that use, rather than only performing a conversion.

official_requirement: Show understanding of character data in internal binary form using ASCII, extended ASCII and Unicode.
official_notes: Students should understand ASCII, extended ASCII and Unicode but are not expected to memorise particular character codes.

official_requirement: Show understanding of how data for a bitmapped image are encoded; perform calculations to estimate the file size for a bitmap image; show understanding of the effects of changing elements of a bitmap image on the image quality and file size.
official_notes: Use and understand the terms pixel, file header, image resolution, screen resolution and colour depth/bit depth. Required effects concern image resolution and colour depth/bit depth.

official_requirement: Show understanding of vector-graphic encoding and justify bitmap or vector storage for a given task.
official_notes: Use drawing object, property and drawing list; a justification must connect bitmap/vector characteristics to the stated application.

official_requirement: Show understanding of how sound is represented and encoded; show understanding of the impact of changing the sampling rate and resolution.
official_notes: Use the terms sampling, sampling rate and sampling resolution. Explain the impact of changing sampling rate and sampling resolution on file size and accuracy; sound-file-size calculation is not stated as a compulsory requirement.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the need for and examples of file compression; show understanding of lossy and lossless compression and justify a method for a given application; show understanding of how a text, bitmap, vector graphic and sound file can be compressed.
official_notes: Run-length encoding (RLE) is the named example in the adjacent Notes and guidance.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the purpose and benefits of networking devices and the characteristics of LANs and WANs.
official_notes: A LAN covers a limited area and is normally managed by one organisation; a WAN connects sites across a large area and commonly uses provider infrastructure. Benefits must identify a shared or centrally managed resource and its consequence.

official_requirement: Explain client-server and peer-to-peer models, their computer roles, benefits and drawbacks, and justify a model for a given situation.
official_notes: Evidence must cover the different computer roles in each model, balanced benefits and drawbacks, and a scenario-linked choice; a topology cannot substitute for a network model.

official_requirement: Show understanding of thin-client and thick-client computers and the differences between them.
official_notes: Thin/thick describes where processing, software and storage reside; it must not be treated as a synonym for client-server/peer-to-peer.

official_requirement: Show understanding of bus, star, mesh and hybrid network topologies.
official_notes: All four named topologies are required. A hybrid combines two or more topology patterns; it is not merely a large network.

official_requirement: Explain how packets are transmitted between two hosts for a given topology and justify topology choice for a given situation.
official_notes: Packet or signal paths must be explicit for bus, star, mesh and hybrid. A justification must link the path and failure behaviour to the scenario.

official_requirement: Show understanding of public and private cloud computing, including the benefits and drawbacks of cloud computing.
official_notes: Public refers to shared provider infrastructure, not unrestricted access to customer data. Private infrastructure is dedicated to one organisation but is not automatically secure.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the differences between wired and wireless networks and the implications of using each.
official_notes: Comparisons must connect physical cable or radio transmission to mobility, installation, interference, shared capacity, reliability or security in a stated use.

official_requirement: Describe copper cable, fibre-optic cable, radio waves including WiFi, microwave and satellite transmission.
official_notes: All named media are required. Explanations must include the signalling method or propagation condition and a use/limitation, not only relative speed.

official_requirement: Describe LAN hardware: switch, server, NIC, WNIC, WAP, cables, bridge and repeater.
official_notes: Every named hardware category is required and must be distinguished by its role; a combined consumer device does not merge the logical functions.

official_requirement: Describe the role and function of a router in a network.
official_notes: A router connects different networks and forwards packets using destination IP addresses and routing information; providing WiFi is not the defining role.

official_requirement: Show understanding of Ethernet and how collisions are detected and handled using CSMA/CD.
official_notes: Carrier sensing occurs before transmission; collision detection occurs after transmission begins. A collision causes stop/jam, random backoff, sensing and retry.

official_requirement: Show understanding of bit streaming, including real-time/on-demand methods and the importance of bit rate and broadband speed.
official_notes: A buffer absorbs short variation but cannot repair a sustained connection rate below the media bit rate. Real-time means live; on-demand means stored content selected by the user.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the differences between the World Wide Web and the internet.
official_notes: The internet is interconnected network infrastructure and protocols; the WWW is one service of linked resources accessed over that infrastructure.

official_requirement: Describe internet-supporting hardware and connections, including modems, PSTN, dedicated lines and cell phone networks.
official_notes: A modem adapts data to access-link signalling. PSTN, dedicated lines and cell phone/cellular networks are distinct connection methods and all are compulsory examples.

official_requirement: Explain IP-address use, including IPv4/IPv6 format, subnetting, device association, public/private and static/dynamic addresses, and security implications.
official_notes: IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 is 129-bit. An address is associated with a network interface on a network. Private addressing reduces direct public reachability but does not guarantee security.

official_requirement: Explain how a URL locates a WWW resource and the role of DNS.
official_notes: A URL may contain scheme, domain, optional port, path and optional query/fragment. DNS resolves the domain name to an IP address; it does not resolve the path or store the resource.

official_requirement: Explain the need for input, output, primary storage, secondary storage and removable storage.
official_notes: Show understanding of the need for input, output, primary memory and secondary storage, including removable storage.

official_requirement: Understand embedded systems and their benefits/drawbacks.
official_notes: Show understanding of embedded systems, including their benefits and drawbacks.

official_requirement: Describe principal operation of laser printer, 3D printer, microphone, speakers, HDD, flash memory, optical reader/writer, touchscreen and VR headset.
official_notes: Describe the principal operations of: laser printer, 3D printer, microphone, speakers, magnetic hard disk, solid state (flash) memory, optical disc reader/writer, touchscreen and virtual reality headset.

official_requirement: Understand why buffers are used.
official_notes: Show understanding of the use of buffers, including temporary storage used to manage different producer and consumer rates.

official_requirement: Distinguish RAM and ROM.
official_notes: Explain the differences between RAM and ROM, including their use in a range of devices and systems.

official_requirement: Explain uses of SRAM and DRAM and reasons for each use.
official_notes: Explain the differences between SRAM and DRAM, including their uses in a range of devices and systems and the reasons for choosing one instead of the other.

official_requirement: Understand PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.
official_notes: Explain the difference between PROM, EPROM and EEPROM, including how each can be programmed or erased.

official_requirement: Distinguish monitoring and control; understand sensors, actuators and feedback.
official_notes: Show understanding of monitoring and control systems, including the difference between monitoring and control, the use of sensors and actuators, and the importance of feedback.

official_requirement: Understand temperature, pressure, infrared and sound sensors and appropriate applications.
official_notes: Required sensor types are temperature, pressure, infra-red and sound; teaching and assessment must connect each sensor to an appropriate application.

official_requirement: Understand NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR and XOR; use symbols/functions/truth tables and convert among problem, expression, circuit and truth table.
official_notes: Use the standard symbols and define the functions of NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR and XOR (EOR); all gates except NOT have two inputs. Construct circuits, truth tables and expressions from each of the other stated representations: problem statement, logic expression, logic circuit and truth table.

official_requirement: Understand Von Neumann architecture and the stored-program concept.
official_notes: Show understanding of the basic Von Neumann model and the stored-program concept: instructions are stored in binary in the same directly accessible memory as data and are fetched for execution.

official_requirement: Understand general- and special-purpose registers: PC, MDR, MAR, ACC, IX, CIR and status register.
official_notes: Distinguish general-purpose and special-purpose registers and explain PC, MDR, MAR, ACC, IX, CIR and status-register roles. Cambridge assembly questions assume ACC is the available general-purpose working register.

official_requirement: Understand ALU, CU, clock and immediate access store (IAS).
official_notes: Show understanding of the purpose and roles of the ALU, CU, system clock and Immediate Access Store (IAS). IAS is directly accessible memory for current instructions and data, not a register or cache.

official_requirement: Understand address, data and control buses.
official_notes: Show how data are transferred between computer-system components using the address bus, data bus and control bus, including their directions and roles in read/write operations.

official_requirement: Understand processor performance factors: processor type, cores, bus width, clock and cache.
official_notes: Show how processor type and number of cores, bus width, clock speed and cache memory can contribute to performance; no single factor guarantees faster execution for every workload.

official_requirement: Understand USB, HDMI and VGA ports.
official_notes: Understand how ports connect peripheral devices, including Universal Serial Bus (USB), High Definition Multimedia Interface (HDMI) and Video Graphics Array (VGA), with accurate signal/use distinctions.

official_requirement: Describe the fetch-execute cycle using register transfer notation.
official_notes: Describe the stages of the Fetch-Execute cycle and use register-transfer notation, including MAR <- PC, MDR <- Memory[MAR], CIR <- MDR and a coherent PC update.

official_requirement: Understand causes/applications of interrupts, ISR, detection and handling.
official_notes: Include possible causes and applications of interrupts, the use of an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), when interrupts are detected during the fetch-execute cycle and the full save-handle-restore sequence.

official_requirement: Distinguish assembly language and machine code.
official_notes: Show the relationship between assembly language and machine code: assembly is a processor-specific symbolic low-level form translated by an assembler into binary instructions defined by the target instruction set.

official_requirement: Describe and apply the stages of a two-pass assembler.
official_notes: Describe the different stages of a two-pass assembler and apply the process to a simple program: pass 1 assigns addresses/builds the symbol table and pass 2 translates with resolved symbols.

official_requirement: Trace a simple assembly-language program.
official_notes: Trace a given simple assembly-language program by recording each executed instruction, register/memory/output changes and taken or not-taken control flow.

official_requirement: Understand instruction groups: data movement, input/output, arithmetic, conditional/unconditional branch and compare.
official_notes: Group the specified instructions as data movement, input/output, arithmetic, unconditional branch, conditional branch and compare operations; classification must follow each instruction's official effect rather than an English guess from its mnemonic.

official_requirement: Use the specified instruction set: LDM, LDD, LDI, LDX, LDR, MOV, STO, ADD, SUB, INC, DEC, JMP, CMP, CMI, JPE, JPN, IN, OUT and END.
official_notes: Use the complete Version 2 instruction set with its specified operands and effects. In particular LDR #n loads IX, CMI <address> is indirect comparison, JPE follows a True comparison and JPN follows a False comparison.

official_requirement: Understand immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative addressing.
official_notes: Use immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative addressing. Relative addressing forms an address from a PC-based instruction address plus an offset; LDR #n remains immediate-to-IX, not relative.

official_requirement: Use AND, OR, XOR, LSL and LSR for bit manipulation, including testing/setting bits with masks.
official_notes: Use AND, OR and XOR masks to test, set, clear and toggle bits, and apply logical, arithmetic and cyclic left/right shifts at a stated fixed width. Include device monitoring/control and distinguish discarded, sign-filled and rotated bits.

official_requirement: Explain why an operating system is required and its memory, file, security, hardware and process management roles.
official_notes: The operating system is required to provide a platform and manage memory, files, security, hardware input/output and peripherals, and processes.

official_requirement: Understand disk formatter, antivirus, defragmentation, disk analysis/repair, compression and backup utilities.
official_notes: Required utility categories are disk formatter, virus checker, defragmentation, disk contents analysis and repair, file compression and backup software.

official_requirement: Understand libraries and benefits of dynamically linked library files.
official_notes: Software under development is often constructed using existing code from program libraries. Explain developer benefits, including the use of dynamically linked library files.

official_requirement: Explain why assembler, compiler and interpreter are needed.
official_notes: An assembler translates assembly language, a compiler translates high-level language, and an interpreter translates and executes high-level language.

official_requirement: Compare compiler and interpreter advantages/disadvantages and justify use.
official_notes: Explain the benefits and drawbacks of a compiler and an interpreter, and justify which translator is appropriate for a stated use.

official_requirement: Understand that Java is partly compiled and partly interpreted.
official_notes: A high-level program may be partly compiled and partly interpreted; Java in console mode is the required example.

official_requirement: Understand IDE features: context-sensitive prompts, dynamic syntax checking, prettyprint, expand/collapse, single-step, breakpoints, variable/expression inspection and report window.
official_notes: IDE evidence must cover coding prompts; dynamic syntax error detection; prettyprint and expand/collapse presentation; and debugging with single stepping, breakpoints, variables, expressions and a report window.

official_requirement: Distinguish data security, privacy and integrity.
official_notes: Distinguish data security, data privacy and data integrity as separate concepts; evidence must not treat confidentiality, lawful/appropriate use and correctness/consistency as interchangeable.

official_requirement: Explain the need for data and computer-system security.
official_notes: Show appreciation of the need for both security of data and security of the computer system; evidence must explain why protecting one layer does not replace the other.

official_requirement: Understand user accounts/passwords, digital signatures, biometrics, firewall, antivirus, anti-spyware and encryption as security measures.
official_notes: Describe security measures for computer systems from a stand-alone PC to a network: user accounts, passwords, digital signatures, biometrics, firewall, anti-virus, anti-spyware and encryption are all required named evidence.

official_requirement: Understand virus, spyware, hackers, phishing and pharming threats.
official_notes: Show understanding of threats posed by networks and the internet, including malware (virus and spyware), hackers, phishing and pharming; all five named threats require direct evidence.

official_requirement: Understand restriction of access to data and computer systems as a risk-reduction method.
official_notes: Describe methods that restrict the risks posed by threats to data and computer systems; evidence must match each control mechanism to the attack route and avoid claims of total prevention.

official_requirement: Explain how encryption and access rights protect data.
official_notes: Describe security methods designed to protect data, including encryption and access rights; evidence must explain their different mechanisms and limitations.

official_requirement: Describe how data validation and data verification help protect the integrity of data; describe and use methods of data validation.
official_notes: Validation and verification reduce input, copying and transfer errors and therefore help protect data integrity. Validation methods include range, format, length, presence, existence and limit checks, plus a check digit.

official_requirement: Understand verification: visual and double entry; parity byte/block and checksum.
official_notes: Describe and use verification during data entry (visual check and double entry) and during data transfer (parity check on a byte, block parity and checksum).

official_requirement: Show understanding of the need for and purpose of ethics as a computing professional.
official_notes: Version 2 requires both the need for professional ethics and its purpose; evidence must connect responsible professional decisions to public interest, competence and accountability.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the importance of joining a professional ethical body, including BCS and IEEE.
official_notes: Version 2 names BCS (British Computer Society) and IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers). Evidence must teach why joining matters, not merely expand the abbreviations or mention a code.

official_requirement: Explain the need to act ethically and the impact of acting ethically or unethically for a given situation.
official_notes: Version 2 requires scenario judgement plus consequences. Evidence must identify stakeholders and explain impacts of both ethical and unethical action; a label or generic list is insufficient.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the need for copyright legislation for software.
official_notes: Version 2 requires the need for copyright legislation, not only a definition. Evidence must connect protected software expression and restricted acts to enforceable permission, revenue or investment.

official_requirement: Explain different software licensing types and justify a licence for a given situation.
official_notes: Version 2 explicitly includes the Free Software Foundation, Open Source Initiative, shareware and commercial software. All four must be taught; a scenario answer must justify permissions, restrictions, cost or support rather than choose by label alone.

official_requirement: Show understanding of artificial intelligence, its applications and its social, economic and environmental impacts.
official_notes: Version 2 requires applications of AI and impacts across all three named dimensions: social, economic and environmental. Evidence must connect an AI mechanism to stakeholder consequences, benefits, harms and a contextual judgement.

official_requirement: Explain limitations of file-based systems and how relational databases address them.
official_notes: Version 2 requires both sides of the comparison: limitations of file-based storage/retrieval and relational-database features that address those limitations. Benefits must be linked to a mechanism rather than asserted generically.

official_requirement: Understand entity/table, record/tuple, field/attribute, primary/candidate/secondary/foreign key, relationships, referential integrity and indexing.
official_notes: Version 2 explicitly names entity, table, record, field, tuple, attribute, primary key, candidate key, secondary key, foreign key, one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many, referential integrity and indexing. Secondary key is retained as a distinct retrieval term, not an alias for an alternate candidate key.

official_requirement: Produce and interpret entity-relationship diagrams.
official_notes: Version 2 requires candidates to use an entity-relationship diagram to document a database design. Evidence must include entities, relationships and cardinality, not merely define entity and attribute.

official_requirement: Understand 1NF, 2NF and 3NF; explain 3NF and produce a normalised design.
official_notes: Version 2 names First, Second and Third Normal Form and separately requires candidates to explain whether given tables are in 3NF and to produce a normalised design from a description, data or tables.

official_requirement: Understand DBMS features: data dictionary, data modelling, logical schema, integrity, security, backup and access rights.
official_notes: Version 2 explicitly requires data management including a data dictionary, data modelling, logical schema, data integrity and data security including backup procedures and access rights for individuals or groups.

official_requirement: Understand the developer interface and query processor.
official_notes: Version 2 names the developer interface and query processor as DBMS software tools whose use and purpose must be understood in practice. They must be distinguished rather than listed without function.

official_requirement: Understand DDL creates/modifies structure, DML queries/maintains data, and SQL is an industry-standard language.
official_notes: Version 2 distinguishes DBMS creation/modification of database structure through DDL from queries and data maintenance through DML, and identifies SQL as the industry standard for both.

official_requirement: Understand a given SQL statement and explain the semantics of its clauses, identifiers, operators and values.
official_notes: Version 2 explicitly requires understanding a given SQL statement. Evidence must show what a statement does to its result or stored data, not only recognise isolated keywords.

official_requirement: Use DDL: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE with CHARACTER/VARCHAR/BOOLEAN/INTEGER/REAL/DATE/TIME, ALTER TABLE, primary and foreign keys.
official_notes: Version 2 requires CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, CHARACTER, VARCHAR(n), BOOLEAN, INTEGER, REAL, DATE, TIME, PRIMARY KEY(field) and FOREIGN KEY(field) REFERENCES Table(Field). Each named item remains core.

official_requirement: Use DML on at most two tables: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT and AVG.
official_notes: Version 2 limits DML scripts to data stored in at most two tables and names SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT and AVG. The course uses explicit INNER JOIN ... ON for two-table core queries.

official_requirement: Use INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE to maintain data.
official_notes: Version 2 names INSERT INTO, DELETE FROM and UPDATE as required data-maintenance statements. Evidence must distinguish adding, removing and changing records and use WHERE when only selected records should be affected.

official_requirement: Understand abstraction, its purpose/benefits and creation of an abstract model.
official_notes: Abstraction is required both as a concept and as a practical modelling skill: explain its need and benefits, then produce an abstract model containing only details essential to the problem.

official_requirement: Use decomposition and express a problem as modules.
official_notes: Decomposition must break a problem into sub-problems and lead to a program module, identified at design level as a procedure or function with a distinct responsibility.

official_requirement: Understand what an algorithm is.
official_notes: An algorithm is a solution to a problem expressed as a sequence of defined steps; the definition requires both the problem-solving purpose and the defined sequence.

official_requirement: Choose meaningful identifier names and construct an identifier table.
official_notes: Students must choose suitable meaningful identifier names and construct an identifier table that records each identifier's name, data type and purpose for the designed algorithm.

official_requirement: Use input-process-output to design pseudocode solutions.
official_notes: Use input, process and output as the design structure for a complete pseudocode solution; the three parts must connect, use meaningful identifiers and satisfy the stated problem.

official_requirement: Understand and use sequence, selection and iteration.
official_notes: The three basic algorithm constructs are sequence, selection and iteration (repetition); students must recognise and use each construct, including combinations of constructs.

official_requirement: Use structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode; convert between representations.
official_notes: Document an algorithm using structured English, a flowchart or pseudocode; write pseudocode from structured English or a flowchart, and draw a flowchart from structured English or pseudocode while preserving the same algorithm.

official_requirement: Use stepwise refinement to develop an algorithm.
official_notes: Use stepwise refinement to develop an algorithm from a high-level solution to a level of detail from which a program can be written; each level must preserve the parent purpose.

official_requirement: Construct and interpret logic statements.
official_notes: Logic statements define parts of an algorithm solution, including decision conditions, loop conditions and Boolean assignments; students must both construct and interpret them.

official_requirement: Understand integer, real, char, string, Boolean and date types and Cambridge pseudocode type names.
official_notes: Select and use appropriate types for a problem solution. The Version 2 Notes name integer, real, char, string, Boolean and date, and require the Cambridge pseudocode type names INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE, ARRAY and FILE.

official_requirement: Understand record purpose and define, read and save record data.
official_notes: A record holds a set of related data of different data types under one identifier. Candidates must write pseudocode to define a record structure, read data from its named fields and save data to its named fields.

official_requirement: Understand array, index, lower bound and upper bound terminology.
official_notes: Use the technical terms associated with arrays, including index, lower bound and upper bound. Bounds define the inclusive valid index range and an index selects one element.

official_requirement: Select one- or two-dimensional arrays for a scenario.
official_notes: Select a suitable one-dimensional (1D) or two-dimensional (2D) array for a given task. One index suits a linear collection; two indexes suit data with a genuine row-column or equivalent two-coordinate relationship.

official_requirement: Write pseudocode using one- and two-dimensional arrays.
official_notes: Write Cambridge pseudocode for 1D and 2D arrays: declare explicit inclusive bounds and an element type, use the required number of indexes, and traverse only valid positions.

official_requirement: Write bubble sort and linear search algorithms.
official_notes: When processing array data, candidates must write a bubble-sort algorithm and a linear-search algorithm. A trace alone is not sufficient evidence of the ability to write each complete algorithm.

official_requirement: Explain the need for files and use text-file pseudocode.
official_notes: Show why files are needed for persistent data beyond one program run, and write Cambridge pseudocode to handle text files consisting of one or more lines, including opening, processing and closing in the correct mode.

official_requirement: Understand the definition and purpose of an abstract data type.
official_notes: An abstract data type (ADT) is a collection of data and a set of operations on those data. Its behaviour is defined independently of a particular storage implementation.

official_requirement: Understand stack, queue and linked-list features; justify a structure.
official_notes: Stack, queue and linked list are examples of ADTs. Describe their key features and justify which structure suits a given situation using LIFO, FIFO or link-based traversal/insertion/deletion evidence.

official_requirement: Add, edit and delete data in the ADTs and implement them using arrays; pseudocode for operations is not required by the syllabus.
official_notes: Use stack, queue and linked list to store data; add, edit and delete data while preserving each ADT rule. Describe array implementations for all three. Candidates are not required to write pseudocode for these ADT operations.

official_requirement: Write pseudocode from a flowchart or structured-English description.
official_notes: Implement and write pseudocode from a given design presented as either a flowchart or structured English.

official_requirement: Use declarations, constants, variables, assignment, arithmetic/logical operations and input/output.
official_notes: Write pseudocode for declaration and initialisation of constants; declaration of variables; assignment of values; expressions using arithmetic or logical operators; input from the keyboard; and output to the console.

official_requirement: Use built-in/library and string functions.
official_notes: Use built-in functions and library routines. Any function not given in the pseudocode guide will be provided; string manipulation functions will always be given in the question.

official_requirement: Use IF/ELSE/nested selection, CASE, count-controlled loops, post-condition and pre-condition loops.
official_notes: Use IF statements, including the ELSE clause and nested IF statements; CASE statements; count-controlled loops; post-condition loops; and pre-condition loops.

official_requirement: Select and justify a suitable loop structure.
official_notes: Justify why one loop structure may be better suited to a problem than another.

official_requirement: Understand and use procedures with parameters passed by reference and by value.
official_notes: Define and use a procedure; explain when the use of a procedure is appropriate; use parameters with none, one or more values passed by reference or by value.

official_requirement: Understand and use functions, including return values in expressions.
official_notes: Define and use a function; explain when the use of a function is appropriate. A function is used in an expression and its return value replaces the function call.

official_requirement: Use precise terminology: procedure/function header, interface, parameter, argument and return value.
official_notes: Use the terminology procedure/function interface, header, parameter, argument and return value, and explain the relationship between these terms.

official_requirement: Write clear and efficient Cambridge pseudocode.
official_notes: Write efficient pseudocode.

official_requirement: Understand why a program-development lifecycle is used; compare waterfall, iterative and RAD models and their stages.
official_notes: Candidates should understand the purpose of a program-development lifecycle and the need for different lifecycles depending on the program being developed. Compare the principles, benefits and drawbacks of waterfall, iterative and Rapid Application Development (RAD). Lifecycle stages are analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance.

official_requirement: Understand, construct and use structure charts, including parameters, and derive pseudocode.
official_notes: Use a structure chart to decompose a problem into subtasks and express the parameters passed between modules, procedures and functions. Describe its purpose, construct one for a given problem and derive equivalent pseudocode from it.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the purpose of state-transition diagrams to document an algorithm.
official_notes: The Version 2 table requires understanding the purpose; it does not require candidates to construct a state-transition diagram.

official_requirement: Identify and correct syntax, logic and runtime errors.
official_notes: Understand different ways of exposing and avoiding faults in a program. Locate and identify syntax, logic and run-time errors in a program and correct identified errors.

official_requirement: Understand dry run, walkthrough, white-box, black-box, integration, alpha, beta, acceptance and stub testing.
official_notes: Describe testing methods and select suitable test data: dry run, walkthrough, white-box, black-box, integration, alpha, beta and acceptance testing, and use of a stub.

official_requirement: Show understanding of the need for a test strategy and test plan and their likely contents.
official_notes: The Version 2 table requires understanding the need and likely contents; it does not require candidates to produce either document.

official_requirement: Select normal, abnormal and extreme/boundary test data.
official_notes: Choose suitable test data for a test plan, including normal, abnormal and extreme/boundary data.

official_requirement: Understand perfective, adaptive and corrective maintenance.
official_notes: Understand the need for continuing maintenance of a program and the differences between perfective, adaptive and corrective maintenance.

official_requirement: Analyse and amend an existing program.
official_notes: Analyse an existing program and make amendments to enhance functionality.
